cues.text: Section ten is an applied case: MetroHealth HMO.
MetroHealth is a growing Nigerian health insurer operating in five states.
At present, its claims processing, customer onboarding and reporting are fragmented across manual processes and incompatible systems.

The organisation now wants several things at once: national expansion, faster claims, better compliance reporting, mobile self-service for its members, and lawful access to patients' treatment history.
On claims in particular, the target is to cut turnaround from ten days to forty-eight hours.
The central alignment problem in this case is that business growth has outpaced IT capabilities.
The company has grown, or plans to grow, faster than its systems and processes can support.
To analyse this properly, we use SAM, the strategic alignment model, and look at four areas in turn.
First, business strategy.
Here the demands are expansion into new markets and better service to members.
Second, IT strategy.
To support that business direction, IT needs integration across its currently incompatible systems, along with secure digital channels through which members and partners can interact.
Third, organisational processes.
These need shared accountability, so that responsibility for outcomes such as claims speed and compliance is not scattered across disconnected teams.
Fourth, infrastructure.
This needs interoperable systems, meaning systems that can exchange and use information with one another.
Now consider a learning example of how MetroHealth might proceed in phases.
In the first phase, the organisation establishes governance, data standards, identity management and baseline measures.
Baselines matter because without knowing where you start, you cannot show improvement later.
In the second phase, it integrates claims and partner systems, and pilots the mobile services on a limited basis.
In the final phase, it expands the capabilities that have proven themselves and optimises analytics.
Governance deserves a closer look.
A steering committee should include representatives from clinical, finance, claims, compliance, IT and leadership.
This breadth ensures that decisions reflect the needs of the whole organisation, and not just the technology function.
There are also practical considerations.
Rural partners may require low-bandwidth interfaces and offline-capable workflows, since reliable connectivity cannot be assumed everywhere.

And privacy controls should restrict access to treatment history according to legitimate purpose and role, so that only people with a proper reason, and an appropriate position, can see sensitive medical information.
Finally, to evaluate progress, use a balanced scorecard.
In this case, it would compare four measures: cost per claim, customer satisfaction, turnaround time, and staff competence.
Together these give a view that is not purely financial or purely technical.
One last note.
What we have just worked through is a teaching illustration of strategic reasoning.
It is not a completed forum submission.
